hints: Consider how increasing temperature affects this equilibrium, remembering the forward reaction is exothermic with a negative ΔH.
The equilibrium must shift to the left on heating, so HI is used up and the 0.80 mol dm-3 value must belong to HI.
Use the 2 to 1 mole ratio from the equation to link the 0.18 fall in HI to the rise in H2, then add it to the starting 1.02.
walkthrough:
**Predict the shift with Le Chatelier**

Think of heat as a product here because the forward reaction gives out heat. Raising the temperature adds heat, so equilibrium shifts left to absorb it, in the endothermic backward direction.

$$\text{H}_2 + \text{I}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI} \quad \Delta H = -9.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Decide which species falls to 0.80**

A left shift means $\text{HI}$ decreases while $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ increase. So the value that falls from 0.98 to 0.80 must be $\text{HI}$.

$$\text{change in [HI]} = 0.98 - 0.80 = 0.18 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \text{ decrease}$$

**Apply stoichiometry to find new [H2]**

From the equation, 2 moles of HI make 1 mole of H2. So the increase in H2 is half the decrease in HI.

$$\text{increase in [H}_2] = 0.18 / 2 = 0.09 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
$$\text{new [H}_2] = 1.02 + 0.09 = 1.11 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$

options.A: 0.80 mol dm-3 is the new concentration of HI, not H2. Heating shifts equilibrium left so HI falls while H2 rises, so H2 cannot be 0.80.
options.B: 0.93 mol dm-3 comes from shifting the wrong way (1.02 - 0.09). This assumes H2 falls on heating, but the exothermic forward reaction means heating favours the backward reaction and H2 must increase.
options.C: HI falls by 0.18 to 0.80, and by the 2HI to 1H2 ratio, H2 rises by 0.09. So new [H2] = 1.02 + 0.09 = 1.11 mol dm-3. This matches the left shift expected on heating.
options.D: 1.20 mol dm-3 comes from adding the full 0.18 to H2 (1.02 + 0.18). This forgets the 2:1 ratio, 2 moles of HI produce only 1 mole of H2, so only half the change applies.
